newsitem.title: USA: Avis franchisee biased against blacks - lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Avis franchisee biased against blacks - lawsuit.

text.p: The owner of several Avis car-rental franchises instructed employees to find reasons not to rent cars to African American customers, according to a class-action lawsuit filed on Tuesday.

The Washington Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, in a discrimination suit seeking unspecified damages, accused the franchise owner of "a vicious, offensive pattern of discrimination over the last 10 years."

The suit, filed in federal court in the Eastern District of North Carolina, claimed that John Dalton, the owner of five franchises in North and South Carolina, instructed employees to find reasons not to rent vehicles to blacks and that Avis executives were aware of the practice and did not stop it.

So far 85 people have joined the suit, which targets Avis Rent A Car Inc. and New Hanover Rent-A-Car Inc. for alleged discrimination beginning in 1986, lead attorney John Relman said. Relman accused Avis executives of "a corporate culture of indifference."

Avis, a unit of HFS Inc., which is based in Parsippany, N.J., issued a statement expressing concern about the allegations. The statement said the company "does not tolerate discriminatory practices of any kind" and had a solid record as an equal-opportunity employer.
"As a franchisor, Avis Inc. is not responsible for any discriminatory practices that may have been carried out by a franchisee or his/her employees," the statement said.
Dalton was not available for comment.

The allegations follow controversy at Texaco Inc., which recently suspended two employees and took away the benefits of two retirees caught on audiotape using racial epithets and planning to destroy documents related to a class-action discrimination lawsuit against the company.

Relman told a news conference that Dalton said in a conversation about a black man who used a corporate account to rent a car and was involved in an accident, "If that damn nigger would have been driving instead of listening to that music, he wouldn't have had the accident."

Former employee Kenneth Ross said all Avis employees at the Wilmington office were told by Dalton to evaluate people who wanted to rent cars based on where they wanted to go, how they were dressed and the colour of their skin.
Asked why nothing had been previously reported by Dalton's employees, Ross said they feared him because of his standing in the community and did not want to lose jobs that paid well.

"The industry standard for a manager in the Wilmington area is about $22,000. I was making between $35 and $40,000. What can I say? I needed the money," said Ross, who said he quit after tiring of long working hours.
Some plaintiffs at the news conference told of how they were denied rental cars in what they could only interpret as discrimination.

"I had reservations made two months in advance for four vans for a family vacation to Disney World in July of last year," Linda Pugh of Tappahanock, Virginia, a travel agent, said. She said the franchise refused to rent her the vans.

Vietta Ratliff of Cheraw, South Carolina, said she encountered the same resistance on Labour Day weekend last year while trying to rent a car at the Avis office in Florence, South Carolina. Lerline Wilson, 54, of Salters, South Carolina, said she was told she was too old.
The plaintiffs said that when they called Avis headquarters to complain, they were told racial complaints had previously been received about the Carolina franchises.
